checks: For fixed epsilon, the derivative of the increment with respect to s is d[(s+epsilon)^(d-1)-s^(d-1)] >= 0, so the bracket is maximized at s=r, including the constant-in-s case epsilon=0. Dividing by r^d is valid for every r>0 and leaves t in [0,1/2]. This reduction needs no positivity hypothesis on the bracket.

On the closed interval both affine arguments of the two powers are nonnegative. Their weighted sum is convex, with derivative d[(1+t)^(d-1)-4(1-2t)^(d-1)]. For d>=2, k=4^(-1/(d-1)) lies strictly between zero and one, so t=(1-k)/(2+k) lies strictly between 0 and 1/2 and gives the global minimum. Substitution gives 1+t=3/(2+k), 1-2t=3k/(2+k), and 1+2k^d=(2+k)/2, yielding the displayed minimum.

Jensen with weights 2/3 at 1 and 1/3 at k gives ((2+k)/3)^(d-1) <= (2+k^(d-1))/3=3/4, equivalently (2+k)^(d-1)<=3^d/4. This gives the lower bound 2, strictly for d>2. At epsilon=0 the two sides are r^d and r^d/2. At epsilon=r/2 the left side is zero and the bracket is at most r^d[2-(3/2)^d]<0.

Independent expansion for d=2 and s=r gives 2(1-2t)^2+(1+t)^2-2=9(t-1/3)^2. At t=1/3, exact rational substitution gives retained mass r^2/9 and bracket 2r^2/9, so every coefficient larger than 1/2 fails at that admissible point.
